body:
Childhood & Early Life

Mary Darby was born in Bristol in 1757 or 1758 (she liked to shave a year off), the daughter of a whaling merchant who was off chasing a doomed scheme to set up a whale fishery in Labrador. He came home, then left for good with a mistress. Her mother ran a school for girls to keep the family afloat, and Mary, a bright and nervy kid, ended up teaching there. She was married off at fifteen to Thomas Robinson, who claimed to have an inheritance. He didn't.

What She Did & Why She's Remembered

She wrote poems, novels, plays and a scorching feminist pamphlet, and was called "the English Sappho" by the papers. She is remembered now for poems that look hard at London poverty and for a memoir that shows how brutally the press could chew up a woman in public. Coleridge admired her and wrote to her; she is one of the people who made the Romantic era, though textbooks long skipped her.

Family Life

Her husband was a gambler and philanderer who ran up debts and put the whole family, baby Maria Elizabeth included, in debtors' prison in 1775. Mary spent about a year there, writing poems. Her daughter Maria became her closest companion and later edited her mother's work. Her own mother was her main support through all of it.

Romantic Life

In 1779 she was spotted on stage as Perdita in The Winter's Tale by the young Prince of Wales, the future George IV. He sent her love letters signed "Florizel" and promised her a fortune. She left the stage and the husband for him, became the most gossiped-about woman in London, and then, within a year, was dropped. The promised money never came. The prince's circle laughed; the caricaturists had a field day. She later had a long, loving, volatile relationship with the soldier Banastre Tarleton, who also proved unreliable and gambled away her money.

Life Until Death

Around 1783, after a fever, she was left partly paralysed from the waist down, probably rheumatic fever complications, and she never walked well again. She kept writing, and wrote harder: a dozen novels, poems under pseudonyms like "Laura Maria" and "Tabitha Bramble", and columns for the Morning Post. She died on 26 December 1800, in Surrey, aged about 43, supposedly of pneumonia, leaving her unfinished memoir to her daughter.

Her Works

Two poems, both public domain from her Poetical Works of 1806. The first is a brisk walk through London waking up, seen by a woman who knows exactly what it costs the people doing the carrying.

Who has not waked to list the busy sounds
Of summer’s morning, in the sultry smoke
Of noisy London? On the pavement hot
The sooty chimney-boy, with dingy face
And tattered covering, shrilly bawls his trade,
Rousing the sleepy housemaid. At the door
The milk-pail rattles, and the tinkling bell
Proclaims the dustman’s office; while the street
Is lost in clouds impervious. Now begins
The din of hackney-coaches, waggons, carts;
While tinmen’s shops, and noisy trunk-makers,
Knife-grinders, coopers, squeaking cork-cutters,
Fruit-barrows, and the hunger-giving cries
Of vegetable-vendors, fill the air.
Now every shop displays its varied trade,
And the fresh-sprinkled pavement cools the feet
Of early walkers. At the private door
The ruddy housemaid twirls the busy mop,
Annoying the smart ’prentice, or neat girl,
Tripping with band-box lightly. Now the sun
Darts burning splendor on the glittering pane,
Save where the canvas awning throws a shade
On the gay merchandise. Now, spruce and trim,
In shops (where beauty smiles with industry)
Sits the smart damsel; while the passenger
Peeps through the window, watching every charm.
Now pastry dainties catch the eye minute
Of humming insects, while the limy snare
Waits to enthrall them. Now the lamp-lighter
Mounts the tall ladder, nimbly venturous,
To trim the half-filled lamps, while at his feet
The pot-boy yells discordant! All along
The sultry pavement, the old-clothes-man cries
In tone monotonous, while sidelong views
The area for his traffic: now the bag
Is slyly opened, and the half-worn suit
(Sometimes the pilfered treasure of the base
Domestic spoiler), for one half its worth,
Sinks in the green abyss. The porter now
Bears his huge load along the burning way;
And the poor poet wakes from busy dreams,
To paint the summer morning.

London's Summer Morning

The second is a two-line-a-beat catalogue of the same city, rich and poor stacked up in couplets, like a Hogarth print in verse.

Pavement slipp’ry, people sneezing,
Lords in ermine, beggars freezing;
Titled gluttons dainties carving,
Genius in a garret starving.
Lofty mansions, warm and spacious;
Courtiers cringing and voracious;
Misers scarce the wretched heeding;
Gallant soldiers fighting, bleeding.
Wives who laugh at passive spouses;
Theatres, and meeting-houses;
Balls, where simp’ring misses languish;
Hospitals, and groans of anguish.
Arts and sciences bewailing;
Commerce drooping, credit failing;
Placemen mocking subjects loyal;
Separations, weddings royal.
Authors who can’t earn a dinner;
Many a subtle rogue a winner;
Fugitives for shelter seeking;
Misers hoarding, tradesmen breaking.
Taste and talents quite deserted;
All the laws of truth perverted;
Arrogance o’er merit soaring;
Merit silently deploring.
Ladies gambling night and morning;
Fools the works of genius scorning;
Ancient dames for girls mistaken,
Youthful damsels quite forsaken.
Some in luxury delighting;
More in talking than in fighting;
Lovers old, and beaux decrepid;
Lordlings empty and insipid.
Poets, painters, and musicians;
Lawyers, doctors, politicians:
Pamphlets, newspapers, and odes,
Seeking fame by diff’rent roads.
Gallant souls with empty purses;
Gen’rals only fit for nurses;
School-boys, smit with martial spirit,
Taking place of vet’ran merit.
Honest men who can’t get places,
Knaves who shew unblushing faces;
Ruin hasten’d, peace retarded;
Candor spurn’d, and art rewarded.

January, 1795

Her longing for fairness came out of a life in which every man who promised to look after her did the opposite. She wrote about the beggars and the starving poets because she had stood close enough to see them.
epi: The Perdita who wrote her way out
quote: And the poor poet wakes from busy dreams, / To paint the summer morning.
